conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How is malignant bone pain from metastases best managed?
options: Analgesics (WHO ladder) plus bisphosphonates (zoledronate) and radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Analgesics (WHO ladder) plus bisphosphonates (zoledronate) and radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Metastatic bone pain is managed with WHO-ladder analgesics plus bisphosphonates (zoledronate reduces skeletal events) and radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets). A pathological fracture is managed with orthopaedic surgery then radiotherapy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which route of administration has 100% bioavailability, the fastest onset, and is unaffected by first-pass metabolism, but carries a risk of phlebitis and air embolism?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Intravenous (IV)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The IV route has 100% bioavailability, the fastest onset (5–10 min), and is not affected by first-pass metabolism, but carries risks of infection, phlebitis and air embolism.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which route is contraindicated in haemophilia due to the risk of a massive haematoma?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Intramuscular (IM)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The intramuscular route is contraindicated in haemophilia because of the risk of a massive haematoma. It has 100% bioavailability with a max volume of 5ml (e.g. adrenaline, glucagon, vaccines).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Why does sublingual GTN act rapidly and avoid the large reduction in drug availability seen with some oral drugs?
options: It bypasses first-pass (hepatic) metabolism, which can otherwise reduce oral drug availability by up to 90%
It is given at a very high dose
It is absorbed in the stomach
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It bypasses first-pass (hepatic) metabolism, which can otherwise reduce oral drug availability by up to 90%
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The sublingual route bypasses first-pass metabolism, giving fast absorption (e.g. GTN, buprenorphine, midazolam). The oral route has variable bioavailability because hepatic first-pass can reduce availability by up to 90% for some drugs.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient in status epilepticus in the community cannot have IV access. Which route/agent is appropriate?
options: Rectal (PR) diazepam — the rectal route has fast onset for patients who can't take orally
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Rectal (PR) diazepam — the rectal route has fast onset for patients who can't take orally
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The rectal route has a fast onset (5–10 min) and is useful for patients who cannot take drugs orally — e.g. diazepam PR for seizures. (Buccal/sublingual midazolam is another seizure option.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: According to NICE maintenance fluid requirements, what is the daily water requirement?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 25–30 mL/kg/day
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NICE maintenance fluid requirements are: water 25–30 mL/kg/day, electrolytes 1 mmol/kg/day of Na, K and Cl, and glucose 50–100 g/day.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A hypovolaemic patient needs a fluid challenge. What is the standard approach, and how is it modified in the elderly or those with heart failure/CKD?
options: 500ml crystalloid STAT over 15 minutes, reduced to 250ml in the elderly/HF/CKD, repeated up to 2000ml then senior review
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 500ml crystalloid STAT over 15 minutes, reduced to 250ml in the elderly/HF/CKD, repeated up to 2000ml then senior review
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: A fluid challenge is 500ml crystalloid STAT (15 mins), reduced to 250ml in the elderly/HF/CKD, repeated up to 2000ml before seeking senior review.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which crystalloid is preferred to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Hartmann's (a balanced crystalloid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Hartmann's is a balanced crystalloid preferred to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis. Colloids (albumin) remain intravascular longer but carry a risk of anaphylaxis and are rarely used.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the maximum safe rate for IV potassium administration, and why?
options: 20 mmol/hour; faster rates risk a fatal cardiac arrhythmia
As a rapid bolus for speed
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 20 mmol/hour; faster rates risk a fatal cardiac arrhythmia
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Potassium should never be given faster than 20 mmol/hour because of the risk of a fatal cardiac arrhythmia, and never as a bolus. Peripheral lines allow a max 40 mmol/L concentration; central lines can give more concentrated K⁺ with continuous cardiac monitoring.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient describes burning, shooting pain with tingling and allodynia. What type of pain is this, and why do opioids work poorly?
options: Nociceptive pain; opioids are highly effective
Neuropathic pain (nerve damage/dysfunction); opioids work poorly, so specific neuropathic agents are used
Acute pain; treat with the WHO ladder alone
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Neuropathic pain (nerve damage/dysfunction); opioids work poorly, so specific neuropathic agents are used
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Burning, shooting, tingling pain with allodynia is neuropathic (nerve damage/dysfunction). Opioids work poorly on neuropathic pain, so specific neuropathic agents are used instead.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How is chronic pain defined by duration?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Pain lasting more than 3 months
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Chronic pain is defined as pain lasting more than 3 months.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which tool is used to identify whether pain has a neuropathic component?
options: The DN4 questionnaire (≥4/10 suggests neuropathic pain)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: The DN4 questionnaire (≥4/10 suggests neuropathic pain)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The DN4 questionnaire identifies neuropathic pain (a score ≥4/10 suggests neuropathic). VAS and NRS measure intensity, and SOCRATES characterises pain.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: According to the WHO analgesic ladder, which drugs are used at Step 2 (moderate pain)?
options: Weak opioids — codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Weak opioids — codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Step 2 (moderate pain) uses weak opioids — codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol — with a non-opioid ± adjuvant. Step 1 is non-opioid (paracetamol ± NSAID) and Step 3 is strong opioids.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents with severe pain. According to WHO ladder principles, what is appropriate?
options: Always start at Step 1 and progress slowly
Leapfrogging is allowed — start directly at Step 3, with a fast-acting rescue dose for breakthrough pain
Start at Step 2 and remain there
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Leapfrogging is allowed — start directly at Step 3, with a fast-acting rescue dose for breakthrough pain
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The ladder principles ('by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual') allow leapfrogging — severe pain can start directly at Step 3, with a fast-acting rescue dose for breakthrough pain. Regular (not just PRN) dosing is used for continuous pain.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which cautions apply to NSAID use?
options: They are safe in all patients
GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, cardiovascular disease and asthma; avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure and co-prescribe a PPI if needed
They must always be co-prescribed with a laxative
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, cardiovascular disease and asthma; avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure and co-prescribe a PPI if needed
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit COX → reduced prostaglandins, with cautions of GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, CVD and asthma. Avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure, and co-prescribe a PPI if needed.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Codeine is a prodrug. Why does its effect vary between individuals?
options: It is metabolised to morphine by CYP2D6, so poor metabolisers get no analgesia and ultra-rapid metabolisers get dangerous morphine levels
It is inactivated by the liver equally in everyone
It is a strong opioid at Step 3
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It is metabolised to morphine by CYP2D6, so poor metabolisers get no analgesia and ultra-rapid metabolisers get dangerous morphine levels
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Codeine is a µ-opioid prodrug converted to morphine by CYP2D6. Poor metabolisers get no analgesia, while ultra-rapid metabolisers get dangerous morphine levels. (Tramadol additionally lowers the seizure threshold and is serotonergic.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What should ALWAYS be co-prescribed when starting an opioid, and why?
options: A PPI, to prevent GI bleeding
A laxative (stimulant ± softener), because constipation is near-universal
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: A laxative (stimulant ± softener), because constipation is near-universal
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: A laxative (stimulant ± softener) should always be co-prescribed with opioids because constipation is near-universal. A PRN antiemetic is also considered when starting.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on opioids becomes drowsy and confused with pinpoint pupils, myoclonus and a reduced respiratory rate. What is the management approach?
options: Reduce the dose or rotate the opioid; give naloxone only if life-threatening
Give naloxone routinely for any toxicity
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Reduce the dose or rotate the opioid; give naloxone only if life-threatening
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Opioid toxicity (drowsiness → confusion, pinpoint pupils, myoclonus, respiratory depression) is managed by reducing the dose or rotating the opioid; naloxone is reserved for life-threatening cases.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with significant renal impairment needs a strong opioid. Why is morphine problematic, and what is preferred?
options: Morphine is fine; use it at standard dose
Morphine accumulates due to active metabolites, so use oxycodone, or fentanyl/buprenorphine
Morphine is too weak; use fentanyl at high dose
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Morphine accumulates due to active metabolites, so use oxycodone, or fentanyl/buprenorphine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In renal impairment, morphine accumulates due to active metabolites, so oxycodone (or fentanyl/buprenorphine) is preferred.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which statement about patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) is correct?
options: It is an oral opioid taken PRN
It is an IV strong opioid, patient-triggered and locked to prevent overdose, needing anaesthetic input with naloxone/antiemetic/atropine available, and other PRN opioids should be avoided alongside
Other PRN opioids should always be co-prescribed
It is used for stable chronic pain only
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It is an IV strong opioid, patient-triggered and locked to prevent overdose, needing anaesthetic input with naloxone/antiemetic/atropine available, and other PRN opioids should be avoided alongside
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: PCA is an IV strong opioid, patient-triggered and locked to prevent overdose. It needs anaesthetic input with naloxone/antiemetic/atropine available, and other PRN opioids should be avoided alongside.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Opioid patches (buprenorphine, fentanyl) are appropriate for which situation?
options: Rapid titration of acute severe pain
Stable chronic pain as background analgesia, not acute titration
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Stable chronic pain as background analgesia, not acute titration
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Opioid patches (buprenorphine, fentanyl) are for stable chronic pain as background analgesia — not for acute titration.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: According to NICE, what are the first-line options for neuropathic pain?
options: One of four: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (switch if one fails)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: One of four: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (switch if one fails)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NICE recommends one of four first-line agents for neuropathic pain — amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin — switching if one fails. Opioids work poorly.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which agent is specifically used for trigeminal neuralgia?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Carbamazepine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Carbamazepine is used specifically for trigeminal neuralgia. Tramadol may be used as rescue only, and capsaicin cream for localised neuropathic pain.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient has chronic primary pain (e.g. fibromyalgia) with no underlying cause. What does NICE recommend? (high-yield)
options: Avoiding most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids) and instead using exercise, psychological therapy (CBT/ACT), and considering an antidepressant (duloxetine)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Avoiding most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids) and instead using exercise, psychological therapy (CBT/ACT), and considering an antidepressant (duloxetine)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: For chronic primary pain (no underlying cause, e.g. fibromyalgia), NICE recommends avoiding most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids) and instead using exercise, psychological therapy (CBT/ACT), and considering an antidepressant (duloxetine) — a high-yield SBA point.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which adjuvant is most appropriate for bone pain?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Bisphosphonates
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Bisphosphonates are the adjuvant for bone pain. Antidepressants/anticonvulsants are for neuropathic pain, corticosteroids for inflammatory/nerve compression/raised ICP, and benzodiazepines for muscle spasm.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How is post-operative pain typically managed?
options: Regular paracetamol + NSAID + opioid (regular MR + PRN immediate-release), local anaesthetic wound infiltration, and PCA, reducing as the patient recovers
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Regular paracetamol + NSAID + opioid (regular MR + PRN immediate-release), local anaesthetic wound infiltration, and PCA, reducing as the patient recovers
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Post-operative pain is managed with regular paracetamol + NSAID + opioid (regular modified-release + PRN immediate-release), local anaesthetic wound infiltration, and PCA, reducing as recovery progresses. Acute severe pain is managed with a titrated IV opioid.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: During which period is the fetus most vulnerable to structural malformations from teratogenic drugs?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: The 1st trimester (organogenesis)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The 1st trimester (organogenesis) is most vulnerable to structural malformations. Some drugs (ACEi, NSAIDs) instead harm specifically in the 2nd/3rd trimester, causing growth/functional/organ damage.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman with a mechanical heart valve needs anticoagulation. Warfarin is teratogenic in pregnancy. What is the safe alternative and why?
options: A DOAC, because it is renally cleared
LMWH, because it does not cross the placenta
Aspirin, because it is a mild agent
Continue warfarin at a lower dose
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: LMWH, because it does not cross the placenta
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Warfarin causes warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia, CNS defects, haemorrhage/fetal loss). LMWH is the safe alternative because it does not cross the placenta. DOACs are also avoided.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman in her second trimester on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension is found to have oligohydramnios. What fetal effects are associated with ACEi/ARBs, and what should she be switched to?
options: Neural tube defects; switch to valproate
Oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure/anuria, skull and lung hypoplasia; switch to labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa
Tooth discolouration; switch to a tetracycline
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure/anuria, skull and lung hypoplasia; switch to labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In the 2nd/3rd trimester, ACEi/ARBs cause oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure/anuria, and skull and lung hypoplasia. Safe alternatives are labetalol, nifedipine, and methyldopa.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which antiepileptic drug is considered the highest-risk in pregnancy, and what characteristic defect does it cause?
options: Sodium valproate; neural tube defects (spina bifida) and fetal valproate syndrome with developmental delay
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Sodium valproate; neural tube defects (spina bifida) and fetal valproate syndrome with developmental delay
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Sodium valproate is the highest-risk AED, causing neural tube defects (spina bifida), fetal valproate syndrome, and developmental delay. Safer alternatives are lamotrigine and levetiracetam.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman with epilepsy is planning pregnancy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Continue valproate at the lowest dose
Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam with folate supplementation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam with folate supplementation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: For epilepsy in pregnancy, avoid valproate and phenytoin and use lamotrigine or levetiracetam with folate. Teratogenic AEDs should ideally be switched pre-conception.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman is inadvertently exposed to lithium in the first trimester. Which characteristic cardiac defect is associated with lithium?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Ebstein's anomaly (a tricuspid valve defect)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Lithium is associated with Ebstein's anomaly (a tricuspid valve cardiac defect). It requires careful specialist review in pregnancy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis wishes to conceive. What advice is correct?
options: Methotrexate is an abortifacient causing multiple malformations and must be stopped ≥3–6 months pre-conception
Stop only in the third trimester
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Methotrexate is an abortifacient causing multiple malformations and must be stopped ≥3–6 months pre-conception
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Methotrexate is an abortifacient causing multiple malformations and should be stopped ≥3–6 months pre-conception.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which drug, associated with severe CNS/cardiac/craniofacial defects, requires patients to be enrolled in a strict pregnancy-prevention programme?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Isotretinoin (a retinoid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Isotretinoin (a retinoid) causes severe CNS/cardiac/craniofacial defects and requires a strict pregnancy-prevention programme.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman needs an antibiotic. Which agent is associated with tooth discolouration and impaired fetal bone growth, and what should be used instead?
options: A tetracycline (e.g. doxycycline); use penicillins/cephalosporins instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: A tetracycline (e.g. doxycycline); use penicillins/cephalosporins instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline) cause tooth discolouration and impaired bone growth (2nd/3rd trimester). Penicillins/cephalosporins are the safe alternatives.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which class of antibiotic is associated with fetal ototoxicity (CN VIII damage → deafness)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin) cause ototoxicity — CN VIII damage leading to deafness.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman in her first trimester has a UTI. Why is trimethoprim avoided, and which agent is preferred?
options: It is a folate antagonist causing neural tube defects; use cefalexin (or nitrofurantoin early, amoxicillin if sensitive)
It causes tooth discolouration; use doxycycline
It is safe and should be used
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It is a folate antagonist causing neural tube defects; use cefalexin (or nitrofurantoin early, amoxicillin if sensitive)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist causing NTDs in the 1st trimester. Cefalexin is preferred (nitrofurantoin can be used early, and amoxicillin if sensitive).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Nitrofurantoin is generally safe earlier in pregnancy but should be avoided at term. Why?
options: It causes neural tube defects at term
It can cause neonatal haemolysis if used at term (3rd trimester)
It causes premature ductus arteriosus closure
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It can cause neonatal haemolysis if used at term (3rd trimester)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Nitrofurantoin can cause neonatal haemolysis if used at term (3rd trimester), so it is avoided then although safe earlier in pregnancy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman near term takes an NSAID for pain. What is the characteristic fetal risk, and what is the safe analgesic alternative?
options: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus (and oligohydramnios); use paracetamol
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus (and oligohydramnios); use paracetamol
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In the 3rd trimester, NSAIDs cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios. Paracetamol is the safe alternative.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman with hyperthyroidism becomes pregnant while on carbimazole. What fetal harm is associated with carbimazole, and what is preferred in the first trimester?
options: Aplasia cutis and choanal/oesophageal atresia; switch to propylthiouracil in the first trimester
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Aplasia cutis and choanal/oesophageal atresia; switch to propylthiouracil in the first trimester
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Carbimazole is associated with aplasia cutis and choanal/oesophageal atresia. Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which historical drug is the archetype of teratogenicity, and what limb malformation does it cause?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Thalidomide; phocomelia (limb defects)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Thalidomide is the historical archetype of teratogenicity, causing phocomelia (limb defects).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which set of drugs is associated with harm specifically in the 2nd/3rd trimester (growth/functional/organ damage)?
options: ACEi/ARB (renal), tetracyclines (teeth/bone), NSAIDs (ductus arteriosus), nitrofurantoin at term (haemolysis)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: ACEi/ARB (renal), tetracyclines (teeth/bone), NSAIDs (ductus arteriosus), nitrofurantoin at term (haemolysis)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: 2nd/3rd trimester harm (growth/functional/organ damage) is characteristic of ACEi/ARB (renal), tetracyclines (teeth/bone), NSAIDs (ductus arteriosus), and nitrofurantoin at term (haemolysis). Valproate, warfarin, methotrexate and retinoids cause 1st-trimester structural malformations.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which general principle should guide prescribing in pregnancy?
options: Always use the highest dose to ensure efficacy
Prescribe only if benefit outweighs risk, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and prefer drugs with a long safety record
Never check pregnancy status before prescribing
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Prescribe only if benefit outweighs risk, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and prefer drugs with a long safety record
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Prescribe in pregnancy only if benefit outweighs risk, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and prefer drugs with a long safety record. Always check pregnancy status, counsel pre-conception, and consult the BNF/UKTIS when unsure.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the overriding principle in the initial management of a poisoned patient?
options: Give a specific antidote immediately in every case
Resuscitation first (A–E), supporting physiology, as most poisonings are managed supportively
Give activated charcoal regardless of the poison
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Resuscitation first (A–E), supporting physiology, as most poisonings are managed supportively
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The poisoned patient is managed with resuscitation first (A–E), supporting physiology rather than relying on antidotes — most poisonings are managed supportively.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Activated charcoal is being considered for a poisoned patient. Which of the following is it useless against?
options: Tricyclic antidepressants taken within an hour
Most oral drugs with a protected airway
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Metals, alcohols, and lithium
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Activated charcoal is given within 1 hour if the airway is protected, but it doesn't bind everything — it is useless for metals, alcohols, and lithium.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following poisons is dialysable by haemodialysis?
options: Salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, and theophylline
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, and theophylline
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The dialysable poisons are salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, and theophylline.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A farm worker presents with pinpoint pupils, salivation, lacrimation, urination, defaecation, bradycardia and bronchorrhoea. Which toxidrome and cause is this?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Cholinergic; organophosphate poisoning
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: This is the cholinergic toxidrome — small pupils (miosis), SLUD, bradycardia and bronchorrhoea ('wet') — caused by organophosphates. The highest-yield discriminator is 'wet + small pupils' = cholinergic.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient is dry, hot, flushed and delirious with large pupils, urinary retention and tachycardia. Which toxidrome is this, and what is a typical cause?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Anticholinergic; TCAs, antihistamines, or atropine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The anticholinergic toxidrome features large pupils (mydriasis), a dry, hot, flushed patient with delirium, retention and tachycardia — caused by TCAs, antihistamines or atropine. 'Dry + large pupils' = anticholinergic.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the single highest-yield discriminator between the cholinergic and anticholinergic toxidromes?
options: 'Wet vs dry': cholinergic = wet + small pupils; anticholinergic = dry + large pupils
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 'Wet vs dry': cholinergic = wet + small pupils; anticholinergic = dry + large pupils
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The 'wet vs dry' rule is the single highest-yield discriminator: cholinergic = wet + small pupils (organophosphates); anticholinergic = dry + large pupils (TCA/antihistamine).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How does paracetamol cause hepatotoxicity, and which patient group is at higher risk?
options: Direct hepatocyte necrosis; risk highest in the young
Via the toxic metabolite NAPQI; higher risk in chronic alcohol use, anorexia/malnutrition, and P450 inducers (reduced glutathione)
By causing cholestasis; risk in obesity
Through an immune reaction; risk in atopic patients
By raising ammonia; risk in renal failure
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Via the toxic metabolite NAPQI; higher risk in chronic alcohol use, anorexia/malnutrition, and P450 inducers (reduced glutathione)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Paracetamol causes hepatotoxicity via NAPQI (a toxic metabolite). Risk is higher in chronic alcohol use, anorexia/malnutrition, and with P450 inducers, because malnutrition depletes glutathione.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents 6 hours after a single (non-staggered) paracetamol overdose. How should treatment be guided?
options: Measure the level at 4 hours and plot on the nomogram; give N-acetylcysteine according to the nomogram
Measure the level immediately at presentation and treat if any level is detectable
Give activated charcoal regardless of timing
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Measure the level at 4 hours and plot on the nomogram; give N-acetylcysteine according to the nomogram
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: For non-staggered overdose, the level is measured at 4 hours and plotted on the nomogram (measuring earlier is unreliable). NAC is given according to the nomogram. Liver damage peaks at 72–96h, and early NAC saves lives.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which set of criteria indicates the need for liver transplant referral in paracetamol overdose (King's College criteria)?
options: pH <7.3 after 24h, OR all three of PT >100s + creatinine >300 + grade 3/4 encephalopathy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: pH <7.3 after 24h, OR all three of PT >100s + creatinine >300 + grade 3/4 encephalopathy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Transplant is indicated if pH <7.3 after 24h, OR all three of PT >100s, creatinine >300, and grade 3/4 encephalopathy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with a salicylate (aspirin) overdose has tinnitus and is hyperventilating. What is the characteristic sequence of acid-base disturbance?
options: Metabolic acidosis first, then respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis first (hyperventilation stimulates the medulla), then metabolic acidosis (lactic acid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Respiratory alkalosis first (hyperventilation stimulates the medulla), then metabolic acidosis (lactic acid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Salicylate overdose causes a mixed disorder: respiratory alkalosis first (aspirin stimulates the medullary respiratory centre), then metabolic acidosis (lactic acid accumulation).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How does urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate help in salicylate overdose?
options: It binds salicylate in the gut
It traps ionised salicylate in the urine, increasing its excretion
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It traps ionised salicylate in the urine, increasing its excretion
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: IV sodium bicarbonate causes urinary alkalinisation, which traps ionised salicylate in the urine and increases its excretion. Haemodialysis is indicated if concentration >700mg/L, metabolic acidosis, ARF, pulmonary oedema, or seizures.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and drowsiness. What is the emergency antidote, and what caution applies?
options: Naloxone (IV/IM); it is short-acting and may need repeat doses or an infusion for long-acting opioids, with risk of re-narcotisation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Naloxone (IV/IM); it is short-acting and may need repeat doses or an infusion for long-acting opioids, with risk of re-narcotisation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The opioid triad (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, drowsiness) is reversed with naloxone (IV/IM), an opioid receptor antagonist. It is short-acting, so may need repeat doses or an infusion for long-acting opioids — monitor for re-narcotisation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with a tricyclic antidepressant overdose has a widened QRS on ECG. What is the first-line treatment and its mechanism?
options: IV sodium bicarbonate; alkalinises plasma, reducing free TCA and narrowing the QRS
Activated charcoal alone regardless of timing
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: IV sodium bicarbonate; alkalinises plasma, reducing free TCA and narrowing the QRS
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: TCA overdose is cardiotoxic (wide QRS, prolonged QTc, risk of torsades). IV sodium bicarbonate is first-line — it alkalinises the plasma, reducing free TCA and narrowing the QRS. Flumazenil should NOT be given (a BZD might coexist; seizure risk).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which antidote reverses benzodiazepine overdose, and what is the key caution?
options: Flumazenil (GABA-A receptor antagonist); caution — may precipitate withdrawal seizures in dependent patients
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Flumazenil (GABA-A receptor antagonist); caution — may precipitate withdrawal seizures in dependent patients
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Benzodiazepine overdose is usually managed supportively; flumazenil (a GABA-A receptor antagonist) is the reversal agent but may precipitate withdrawal seizures in dependent patients.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient rescued from a house fire has headache and confusion, with pink mucosae and a normal-reading pulse oximeter. Why is the SpO₂ misleading, and what is the treatment?
options: SpO₂ is accurate; give room air
Pulse oximetry can't distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ is falsely normal; treat with 100% O₂ via non-rebreathe mask (and hyperbaric O₂ if severe/pregnant)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Pulse oximetry can't distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ is falsely normal; treat with 100% O₂ via non-rebreathe mask (and hyperbaric O₂ if severe/pregnant)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In CO poisoning, SpO₂ is falsely normal because oximetry can't distinguish CO-Hb (co-oximetry is needed). Treatment is 100% O₂ via non-rebreathe mask (shortens CO-Hb t½ from 5h to 90min), with hyperbaric O₂ if severe or in pregnancy. Cherry-red skin is a late/post-mortem sign.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: In organophosphate poisoning, what are the first-line and additional antidotes?
options: Atropine first-line (titrated until secretions dry) and pralidoxime (regenerates AChE) if given early
Sodium bicarbonate first-line; charcoal if late
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Atropine first-line (titrated until secretions dry) and pralidoxime (regenerates AChE) if given early
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing ACh excess (SLUD, bradycardia, miosis, bronchospasm). Atropine is first-line, titrated until secretions dry, and pralidoxime (which regenerates AChE) is given early.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient who drank antifreeze develops CNS depression then a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and renal failure. What is the poison, and how is it treated?
options: Ethylene glycol; treat with fomepizole (or ethanol) plus haemodialysis
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Ethylene glycol; treat with fomepizole (or ethanol) plus haemodialysis
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) causes initial CNS depression, then a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and renal failure (converted to oxalic acid). Treatment is fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor, first-line) or ethanol infusion, plus haemodialysis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents with a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and visual loss/blindness after ingesting a toxic alcohol. Which poison is this, and what is the mechanism of the eye toxicity?
options: Ethylene glycol; oxalate crystals in the eye
Methanol; optic nerve toxicity from formic acid
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Methanol; optic nerve toxicity from formic acid
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Methanol poisoning presents like ethylene glycol but with the hallmark of visual loss/blindness due to optic nerve toxicity from formic acid. The pairing is: glycol → renal failure, methanol → blindness. Treatment is fomepizole/ethanol + haemodialysis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A toddler with accidental iron overdose has vomiting and haematemesis, then a latent phase, then shock and hepatotoxicity. What is the antidote, and does charcoal help?
options: Desferrioxamine (a chelator); charcoal does not bind iron
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Desferrioxamine (a chelator); charcoal does not bind iron
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Iron overdose progresses through GI symptoms → latent phase → shock + hepatotoxicity (with later bowel strictures). The antidote is desferrioxamine (a chelator); activated charcoal does not bind iron.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on lithium becomes dehydrated after starting a thiazide and develops a coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion. Which factors precipitate lithium toxicity, and how is it managed?
options: Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi and thiazides; managed with IV fluids (0.9% saline) and haemodialysis if severe, as there is no specific antidote
Precipitated by exercise; managed with flumazenil
Precipitated by high protein intake; managed with charcoal
Precipitated by alkalosis; managed with naloxone
Precipitated by nothing; it has a wide therapeutic index
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi and thiazides; managed with IV fluids (0.9% saline) and haemodialysis if severe, as there is no specific antidote
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index; toxicity (coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures, renal impairment) is precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi and thiazides. There is no specific antidote — manage with IV 0.9% saline and haemodialysis if severe.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: During a regional anaesthetic, a patient develops perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures and cardiac arrest after inadvertent IV bupivacaine. What is the antidote?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) — the 'lipid sink'
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Local anaesthetic toxicity (perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures, cardiac arrest, e.g. from inadvertent IV bupivacaine) is treated with IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) — the 'lipid sink'.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient rescued from a house fire has a high lactate, cardiovascular collapse, reduced GCS and a bitter-almond smell. What is the poison, and its antidote?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Cyanide; hydroxocobalamin (or dicobalt edetate)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Cyanide poisoning (smoke inhalation/industrial) presents with headache, reduced GCS, high lactate, cardiovascular collapse and a classic bitter-almond smell. The antidote is hydroxocobalamin (or dicobalt edetate) — consider in smoke-inhalation victims with high lactate + collapse.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on an SSRI is given tramadol and develops tremor, clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils and hyperthermia. What is the diagnosis, and its management?
options: Serotonin syndrome; supportive care (IV fluids, benzodiazepines), with cyproheptadine or chlorpromazine if severe
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Serotonin syndrome; supportive care (IV fluids, benzodiazepines), with cyproheptadine or chlorpromazine if severe
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity (e.g. SSRI + tramadol) — clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils, hyperthermia. Management is supportive (IV fluids, BZDs for agitation), with cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2 antagonist) or chlorpromazine if severe.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How can serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) and the anticholinergic toxidrome be distinguished by neurological signs?
options: Serotonin syndrome = clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia (antipsychotics); anticholinergic = dry/flushed/normal reflexes
Serotonin syndrome causes rigidity; NMS causes clonus
Anticholinergic causes hyperreflexia; NMS causes flushing
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Serotonin syndrome = clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia (antipsychotics); anticholinergic = dry/flushed/normal reflexes
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Serotonin syndrome shows clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS shows lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia (from antipsychotics); the anticholinergic toxidrome is dry/flushed with normal reflexes.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with a beta-blocker overdose has refractory bradycardia not responding to atropine. Which antidote is used, and by what mechanism?
options: High-dose glucagon; increases cAMP independent of beta-receptors
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: High-dose glucagon; increases cAMP independent of beta-receptors
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In beta-blocker overdose, atropine is used for bradycardia, and high-dose glucagon increases cAMP independent of beta-receptors. (Calcium gluconate is used for calcium-channel blocker overdose.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following best defines an adverse drug reaction (ADR)?
options: Any harm from a drug, including from a prescribing error
A noxious and unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses, distinct from overdose/toxicity and medication errors
A response only occurring after an overdose
A harmless expected effect of a drug
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: A noxious and unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses, distinct from overdose/toxicity and medication errors
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: An ADR is a noxious + unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses — distinct from overdose/toxicity and from medication errors. (An adverse drug event is the broader term that includes harm from medication error.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How does an 'adverse drug event' differ from an ADR?
options: An adverse drug event is any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error, and is therefore broader than an ADR
An adverse drug event only occurs at high doses
An adverse drug event excludes medication errors
An ADR is broader than an adverse drug event
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: An adverse drug event is any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error, and is therefore broader than an ADR
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: An adverse drug event is any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error, making it broader than an ADR (which occurs at normal doses). A side effect is a known, often predictable secondary effect — a subset of ADRs.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following meets the MHRA definition of a serious ADR?
options: An ADR that causes or prolongs hospitalisation
A minor rash that resolves quickly
Any side effect listed in the BNF
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: An ADR that causes or prolongs hospitalisation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The MHRA defines a serious ADR as one that is fatal, life-threatening, disabling/incapacitating, causes/prolongs hospitalisation, causes a congenital abnormality, or is otherwise medically significant.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on a β-blocker develops bradycardia, and another on insulin develops hypoglycaemia. Which Rawlins-Thompson type do these represent?
options: Type A (Augmented) — dose-dependent, predictable exaggeration of the drug's action
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type A (Augmented) — dose-dependent, predictable exaggeration of the drug's action
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type A (Augmented) ADRs are dose-dependent, predictable exaggerations of the drug's action, with low mortality — e.g. β-blocker → bradycardia, opioid → respiratory depression, insulin → hypoglycaemia, anticoagulant → bleeding. Type A is the commonest.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient develops anaphylaxis after penicillin, and another develops Stevens-Johnson syndrome on carbamazepine. Which Rawlins-Thompson type is this, and what are its features?
options: Type B (Bizarre) — not dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated, high mortality
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type B (Bizarre) — not dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated, high mortality
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type B (Bizarre) ADRs are not dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated, and carry high mortality — e.g. penicillin anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia, carbamazepine → SJS, and Reye's syndrome with aspirin.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on long-term steroids develops osteoporosis and Cushing's features. Which type of ADR is this?
options: Type C (Chronic/Continued) — dose and time-dependent with prolonged use
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type C (Chronic/Continued) — dose and time-dependent with prolonged use
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type C (Chronic/Continued) ADRs are dose- and time-dependent, occurring with prolonged use — e.g. steroids → osteoporosis/Cushing's, and bisphosphonates → osteonecrosis of the jaw.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Thalidomide causing teratogenesis, and tardive dyskinesia appearing after long-term antipsychotic use, are examples of which ADR type?
options: Type D (Delayed) — appears long after exposure
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type D (Delayed) — appears long after exposure
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type D (Delayed) ADRs appear long after exposure — e.g. teratogenesis (thalidomide), carcinogenesis (secondary malignancy after chemotherapy/radiotherapy) and tardive dyskinesia. (Carbimazole → agranulocytosis is instead a Type B (Bizarre), idiosyncratic reaction.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient who abruptly stops long-term steroids develops an adrenal crisis. Which Rawlins-Thompson type is this?
options: Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) — on stopping, especially abruptly
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) — on stopping, especially abruptly
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) ADRs occur on stopping a drug, especially abruptly — e.g. steroid withdrawal → adrenal crisis, benzodiazepine/opioid withdrawal, and β-blocker rebound.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the key conceptual split between Type A and Type B ADRs, and how does management differ?
options: Type A is immune and Type B is dose-dependent; both need the drug stopped
Type A is predictable + dose-dependent (managed by dose adjustment); Type B is unpredictable + immune (often need to stop + avoid the drug)
Both are unpredictable and require avoidance
Type A occurs only on withdrawal; Type B on starting
There is no meaningful difference in management
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type A is predictable + dose-dependent (managed by dose adjustment); Type B is unpredictable + immune (often need to stop + avoid the drug)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type A = predictable + dose-dependent (the bulk of ADRs, managed by dose adjustment); Type B = unpredictable + immune (often needing the drug stopped and avoided).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for ADRs?
options: Young healthy adults on a single drug
Polypharmacy, extremes of age, organ impairment, female sex, and genetic factors (e.g. CYP polymorphisms, G6PD)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Polypharmacy, extremes of age, organ impairment, female sex, and genetic factors (e.g. CYP polymorphisms, G6PD)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Risk factors for ADRs include extremes of age (altered PK), polypharmacy (interaction risk), organ impairment (renal/hepatic), female sex, genetic factors (CYP polymorphisms, G6PD), and multiple comorbidities.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: When assessing whether a drug caused a reaction, symptoms improve when the drug is stopped and recur when it is restarted. What are these two steps called?
options: Dechallenge (improvement on stopping) and rechallenge (recurrence on restarting)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Dechallenge (improvement on stopping) and rechallenge (recurrence on restarting)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Causality assessment uses the temporal relationship, the known reaction profile, improvement on stopping (dechallenge) and recurrence on restarting (rechallenge), and exclusion of other causes — formalised by scales such as Naranjo.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which drug–ADR pairing is a recognised 'classic culprit'?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: ACE inhibitors → cough/angioedema
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Classic culprit ADRs include ACE inhibitors → cough/angioedema, statins → myopathy, amiodarone → multi-organ effects, and methotrexate → marrow/liver toxicity.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the primary purpose of the Yellow Card scheme, and who runs it?
options: Pre-marketing clinical trial approval, run by NICE
Post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing), run by the MHRA (+ Commission on Human Medicines)
Prescription cost monitoring, run by the NHS
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing), run by the MHRA (+ Commission on Human Medicines)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The Yellow Card scheme is the UK system for post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing), run by the MHRA and the Commission on Human Medicines since 1964. It detects rare or delayed ADRs that trials are too small/short to find.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Who is permitted to submit a Yellow Card report, and is proof of causation required?
options: Only doctors, and causation must be proven
Anyone — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers — voluntarily, on suspicion, with no proof of causation needed
Only hospital pharmacists, with proof required
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Anyone — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers — voluntarily, on suspicion, with no proof of causation needed
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Anyone can report — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers — voluntarily. No proof of causation is needed; reports are made on suspicion.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: For a newly-licensed drug marked with a black triangle (▼), which reactions should be reported via Yellow Card?
options: All reactions, however minor, because the drug is under additional monitoring
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: All reactions, however minor, because the drug is under additional monitoring
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The black triangle (▼) marks newly-licensed drugs/vaccines (and biosimilars) under intensive/additional monitoring — all reactions should be reported, however minor.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: For an established (non-black-triangle) drug, which suspected ADRs should always be reported?
options: All serious suspected ADRs (even if already well-recognised), all suspected ADRs in children (<18, even if off-label), suspected ADRs in pregnancy, and delayed reactions
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: All serious suspected ADRs (even if already well-recognised), all suspected ADRs in children (<18, even if off-label), suspected ADRs in pregnancy, and delayed reactions
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Always report: all serious suspected ADRs to established drugs (even if well-recognised), all suspected ADRs in children (<18, even off-label), suspected ADRs in pregnancy (however minor), and delayed reactions such as cancers/fibrosis (even years later).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following is reportable via the Yellow Card scheme?
options: Reactions to any therapeutic agent — including OTC/self-medication, vaccines, blood products, radiographic contrast, and herbal/complementary products
Only drugs bought in a pharmacy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Reactions to any therapeutic agent — including OTC/self-medication, vaccines, blood products, radiographic contrast, and herbal/complementary products
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Yellow Card reporting covers reactions to any therapeutic agent — prescribed and OTC/self-medication, vaccines, blood products, radiographic contrast, and herbal/complementary products — not just prescribed drugs.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which set of measures helps minimise ADRs in prescribing?
options: Maximise the number of drugs and avoid taking a history
Take a full drug + allergy history, avoid polypharmacy/deprescribe, check interactions, start low and go slow in the elderly/organ impairment, and reconcile medications at transitions of care
Prescribe high doses from the outset in the elderly
Never document allergies to save time
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Take a full drug + allergy history, avoid polypharmacy/deprescribe, check interactions, start low and go slow in the elderly/organ impairment, and reconcile medications at transitions of care
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: ADRs are minimised by taking a full drug + allergy history (incl. OTC/herbal), avoiding polypharmacy (deprescribing), checking interactions (BNF), starting low and going slow in the elderly/organ impairment, using the fewest drugs, monitoring high-risk drugs, documenting/communicating allergies, and medication reconciliation at transitions of care.
